title: Lessons from the First Great Enrollment Decline
author: Parker Baxter
summary: Parker Baxter argues that school district leaders today are repeating the mistakes of their predecessors during the 1972 to 1989 enrollment decline, when districts postponed hard decisions, kept hiring and muddled through. He gives historical cases (Cleveland, New York, Chicago) and current ones (Austin, the Adams 12 district in Colorado, Poudre Valley), showing staffing rising while students leave and layoffs eventually falling on junior teachers through last-in-first-out rules. The mechanics are fixed costs, a growth-oriented operating model, and community resistance to closures, which produce a budget paradox where per-pupil spending rises as quality falls. Baxter rejects the old research conclusion that incremental change is the only viable response and says it leads to slow starvation. He calls for public leadership that accepts tradeoffs, restructures staffing and funding, and puts student achievement ahead of system stability.
points: Districts facing falling enrollment tend to delay, add staff and drain reserves, repeating the pattern of the 1970s and 1980s.
Fixed costs, contracts and growth-era structures create a budget paradox in which per-pupil spending rises while service quality falls.
Last-in-first-out layoffs push cuts onto newer teachers regardless of performance, with equity and diversity consequences.
Muddling through postpones conflict but risks a miasma in which a district cannot resolve deadlocks and hollows out electives and then core programs.
The remedy is leadership that makes retrenchment explicit, redesigns staffing and compensation, and prioritises achievement over adult comfort.
quotes: How well do institutional leaders learn from the lessons of the past? If school districts are the institutions in question, the answer is: not well at all.

Between fall 2019 and fall 2024, enrollment in public elementary and secondary schools fell nationally by 1.4 million students (2.8 percent). Forty states have experienced declines, and enrollment is projected to keep dropping—by an additional 2.7 million students by 2031 and even further by 2050.

Why do districts often avoid or delay responding to declining enrollments? Because managing contraction is much more difficult than managing growth. District leaders must confront political conflict, deep-seated professional norms, and internal bureaucratic resistance.
In Austin, Texas, the district has lost 20 percent of its enrollment, more than 17,000 students, over the last 15 years and now faces a deficit amounting to 20 percent of its budget.

During periods of growth, districts add new programs, hire additional staff and administrators, and create new layers of organizational authority. These increments become embedded in the system, making it difficult to cut them later.
Muddling through may postpone conflict, but it can also result in a slow and painful death from malnutrition.

Declining enrollment creates a zero-sum dynamic with no slack resources and clear winners and losers. This dramatically intensifies conflict among stakeholders. Growth can mask errors in judgment, but the management of decline requires leaders who can identify challenges before they become crises and diffuse conflict among competing interests.
Education leaders must have the courage to acknowledge that the traditional model was not designed for retrenchment and must be reinvented for flexibility and adaptation.
